newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Weak Wall St damps Eurobourses, dollar steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Weak Wall St damps Eurobourses, dollar steady.

text.p: Another lower start on Wall Street -- which closed with losses for the third time in a row on Friday -- jolted already nervous European bourses on Monday and pushed them all down.

London had already been weaker during the European morning but Paris and Frankfurt had shown moderate gains. Shortly after New York opened the Dow had tumbled nearly 50 points and French and German stocks quickly slid into the minus column. The Dow recovered slightly later.
In London the blue chip FTSE index slipped back below 4,300 points.
"We've done fairly well to brush off the Street's weakness but if it goes down again we'll go with it," one dealer predicted shortly before Wall Street opened for business.

"Wall Street outperformed us on the way up and it will probably fall further than us if it continues to drop," the dealer said. "But that doesn't mean we can keep bouncing back when the Street falls."
One big faller was NatWest Bank, as the stock went ex-dividend and in reaction to news last Friday that it had lost 50 million pounds ($81 million) on options trading.
Political worries ahead of a British election, due by May, were also unsettling investor sentiment, dealers said.

"After last week's by-election (which the ruling Conservative Party lost by a big margin) people are starting to focus on the fact of a change of government," the head of trading at a major investment bank said.

"That, added to Wall Street's weakness, is keeping people away. Essentially there is no reason to buy this market at the moment. I think we could see the FTSE come off another 100 points before the buyers return," he said.
Markets on both sides of the Atlantic are expected to remain nervous this week, with key U.S. data and more of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony looming.
Greenspan concludes his testimony on Wednesday. Last week he sent stock markets sharply lower with a warning that Wall Street's recent rise has "raised questions of sustainability."

Analysts said the February U.S. employment report on Friday would also keep markets on edge this week though. U.S. consumer spending figures on Monday showed the strongest pickup since last October, adding to the feeling the Federal Reserve may soon hike interest rates.

In Frankfurt, German shares which ended floor trading four points up before New York opened, slipped about a quarter of a percentage point under the influence of Wall Street in later electronic trade.
Dealers said it had been an uninspired bourse session, with buying interest held back by Wall Street's poor performances towards the end of last week.

It was a similar story on the Paris bourse. French shares were higher in the morning, drawing some comfort from the strong dollar, which makes exports more competitive, but they dropped back into negative territory after Wall Street's lower start.

On the currency front, the dollar was off its highs and steady above 1.69 marks. It had firmed in early trading after a German Sunday newspaper report said a relentless rise in German unemployment continued in February.
Sharply divergent employment trends in Germany and the United States in recent months have been among the key driving forces behind the dollar surge against the mark this year.
News of higher German jobless numbers would makes it more difficult for Germany to meet 1997 budget deficit targets necessary to join a European single currency in 1999.
Jitters about a possible delay to the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) have weakened the Italian lira and Spanish peseta over the past week and the downward pressure continued on Monday.

A vigourous verbal defense of the EMU timetable from a range of European officials helped calm early market jitters and the lira rallied from lows alongside speculation of central bank intervention. The Bank of Spain too was seen selling marks.

Both Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer and European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy said EMU delay rumours were nonsense. Tietmeyer said he would be delighted to have Italy join EMU if it met the economic criteria.
Meanwhile in Athens, the Greek bourse plunged 7.45 percent, a record fall for a single day as investors sold shares across-the-board.
Monday's fall took investor losses over the past three sessions 1.2 trillion drachmas ($4.51 billion).

Stunned brokers debated whether the fall was caused by civil strife in neighbouring Albania, a capital market commission warning which many claim pulled the rug from under the market or simply valuation physics pointing to a correction.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was at 1.6925 marks and 120.70 yen, compared with 1.6885 and 120.88 in late European trade on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1600 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 5.3 points at 4,303.0.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 6.39 points at 2,601.16.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed up 4.22 points at 3,263.86.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed fixed at $362.15 compared with London's previous close of $358.45. Silver was at 532 cents.
($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
